::: {.why}
Nine rehearsals since day 203 have made it fluent and probably not shorter, and the failure mode of an academic presenting to a quantitative audience is context that the audience does not need.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Deliver the presentation in five minutes with one result leading and the method reduced to two sentences.
- Answer three hostile follow-up questions about the result's robustness.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Cut rather than polish: lead with the result, give the method in two sentences, and spend the remaining time on why the result is credible and what would falsify it. A quantitative audience wants the estimate, the uncertainty and the threat to validity, in that order, and nothing about the biological background.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Prepare for the follow-ups you will actually get: how do you know it is causal, what is the effect size and is it meaningful, and what would have made you not believe it. Write and rehearse the answer to each, since they are the same three questions asked of any empirical claim and you will get them in every interview.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
A five-minute presentation recorded, leading with the result, plus rehearsed answers to three robustness questions.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Present your genetics research in five minutes to someone quantitative who knows no biology. Which single result do you lead with?
:::
